LoopCaption.growMultiply: {count}% bigger every bounce until it fills the circle
LoopCaption.growMultiplyFact: Each bounce makes the ball {count}% bigger, so it grows exponentially: the size doubles every few bounces, the bounces come faster and faster, and the last few fill most of the circle.
LoopCaption.growAdd: {count} px bigger every bounce until it fills the circle
LoopCaption.growApproach: {count}% closer to the wall with every bounce
LoopCaption.starChords: {count} balls, one circle, every star closing on the same frame
LoopCaption.starChordsOne: {count} ball, one circle, one star closing on itself
LoopCaption.starChordsFact: A star polygon is what a ball draws when every bounce moves it the same number of points round the rim. Each straight line stays the same distance from the centre, so a circle appears in the middle that no ball ever touches. Every ball here moves at the one speed that finishes its star in the same time as the others.
LoopCaption.hoops: {count} hoops spinning faster and faster: the beads climb in order, the biggest hoop first
LoopCaption.hoopsOne: {count} hoop spinning faster and faster, until its bead starts to climb
LoopCaption.hoopsFact: Why in that order? A bead on a turning hoop rests where gravity and the outward pull of the spin balance. Below a critical spin, √(g/R), that point is the bottom; above it, the balance point moves up the hoop and keeps rising as the spin grows. A hoop of 75 cm radius gets there at about 0.58 turns a second, one of 25 cm needs almost a full turn a second, so the beads leave their bottoms from the outside in.
LoopCaption.chaosFan: {count} pendulums start a hair apart, then the film runs backwards
LoopCaption.chaosFanFact: Why do they split? In a double pendulum any small difference in the start grows exponentially, doubling roughly every fraction of a second, so pendulums released almost together only stay together for a few seconds. Edward Lorenz called this the butterfly effect. The way back is the recording played in reverse: run the physics backwards from the end instead and the tiniest rounding error would grow just as fast, and no pendulum would make it home.
LoopCaption.phaseSpiral: {count} rings, each gaining one lap on the next: watch the spiral straighten into one line
LoopCaption.phaseSpiralFact: Ring n goes round n times a cycle, so every ring gains exactly one lap on its neighbour. In between, the dots wind into a spiral and pass through interference patterns; at the end of the cycle every lap count is a whole number at the same instant, and the spiral straightens into one line. It is the same arithmetic as a pendulum wave.
LoopCaption.colourSort: {count} mixed balls, sorted by their own rings
LoopCaption.colourSortFact: Each ring's gates only open outwards, and never for balls of the ring's own colour. So the core's colour can never leave it, the next one gets past the first ring but not its own, and the outermost colour makes it all the way out: mix them up and they sort themselves into a bullseye.
LoopCaption.ellipseFoci: {count} balls fired from one focus, all landing on the other together
LoopCaption.ellipseFociFact: An ellipse has two foci. A shot from one bounces off the wall straight through the other, whichever way it goes, and every one of those paths is the same length – so a whole volley fired at once arrives at the other focus at the same instant. It's why a whisper at one focus of an elliptical room is heard clearly at the other.
LoopCaption.beatMachineMarbles: {count} tuned bars, and every note is a marble
LoopCaption.beatMachineMarblesFact: Each marble drops from its tube at exactly the moment that lets gravity land it on its bar on the beat: a fall of height h takes √(2h/g), so it leaves that long before its note. Then the floor, the lift and the top rail bring it back to its own tube. The tune is original.
LoopCaption.beatMachineStairsFact: Every hop is the same arc and takes exactly one beat: the gravity and the take-off speed are worked out from the tempo, the drop of a step and the height of the arc. After the last step the ball rides the return track back to the top, landing on the first step just as the next phrase begins.
LoopCaption.funnelSpin: watch the ring of {count} spin up as it drops
LoopCaption.funnelSpinFact: A marble rolling round a funnel keeps nearly all of its spin while friction drains its energy and lets it sink. The same spin on a tighter circle is a faster lap – the reason a figure skater spins faster pulling their arms in – so every ring here laps about eleven times faster at the bottom than on the rim.
LoopCaption.brickRebuild: we smashed the logo: {count} bricks, then put every one back
LoopCaption.brickRebuildFact: Every fourth brick that breaks adds another ball, so the smash starts slow and turns exponential: a handful of balls becomes hundreds, the last corner bricks hold out longest, and then the picture flies back together one colour at a time.
LoopCaption.brickRebuildCapsulesFact: Every gold capsule the paddle catches splits every ball in play into three. Three catches turn 3 balls into 81; five turn them into 729 – the same arithmetic as folding a sheet of paper in three.
LoopCaption.brickRebuildKaleidoscope: only {count} of these balls are real
LoopCaption.brickRebuildKaleidoscopeFact: The rest are reflections: the real balls bounce inside one wedge of the circle with mirror walls, and every brick they break is broken in every mirrored copy too – so the mosaic always stays perfectly symmetric, like the view down a kaleidoscope.
LoopCaption.drawingMachineHarmonographFact: One pendulum swings the pen left and right, one up and down, one round in a circle. Friction drains them, so the drawing shrinks toward the middle. The first two are tuned a little apart, so they slowly drift in and out of step and the shape keeps twisting.
LoopCaption.drawingMachineEarthVenus: earth and venus draw this every {count} years
LoopCaption.drawingMachineEarthVenusFact: Venus goes round the Sun 13 times in almost exactly the time Earth goes round 8, so every 8 years the two planets are back where they started. In between, Venus passes between us and the Sun 5 times, each 144° further round: join those points up and you get a pentagram. The real ratio is off by about 2.5 days a cycle. This one is exact, so the loop closes.
LoopCaption.drawingMachineOrbits: two planets, one line every few days, {count} years
LoopCaption.drawingMachineOrbitsFact: A straight line joins the two planets every few days and stays. Their periods are a whole-number ratio, so after the cycle both are back where they started and the flower closes.
LoopCaption.perfectFitPentoFact: the 12 pentominoes cover 60 squares. they fill a 6×10 box 2,339 different ways, 5×12 1,010 ways and 4×15 368 ways. 3×20 has only 2 solutions, and neither can be built by dropping pieces straight down, so it isn't here.
LoopCaption.perfectFitTetris: {count} pieces, not one out of place
LoopCaption.perfectFitTetrisFact: every piece falls straight down in its final column and rotation. four sections end in a four-line perfect clear, then the last 30 pieces build 12 full rows that clear together: 280 squares, 28 lines, an empty well.
LoopCaption.waveTankFact: One gap turns a straight wave into a fan. Two gaps make two fans that overlap: where crests line up the water climbs, where a crest lands on a trough it goes flat, and quiet stripes run across the tank. Seven gaps only agree in a handful of directions, so the water leaves as narrow beams, which is how the fine grooves of a CD split light into colours. Thomas Young saw these stripes with sunlight in 1803, and they helped show that light is a wave. The bells along the front sound out the water under them: the beams ring, the stripes stay silent.
LoopCaption.waveTankPointsFact: Two sources bobbing in step send out rings that cross. Where a crest of one meets a trough of the other the water stays flat along curved quiet lines. In between it swells twice as high. The bells along the front fall silent wherever a quiet line reaches them.

ColourSort.canvasTitle: each ring stops only its own colour
ColourSort.canvasTitleOwnOnly: each ring lets out only its own colour
ColourSort.canvasSubtitle: gates open outwards, never for the ring's own colour
ColourSort.canvasSubtitleOwnOnly: gates open outwards, only for the ring's own colour
ColourSort.canvasSubtitleBothWays: gates open both ways, never for the ring's own colour
ColourSort.csDesc: Balls of every colour start packed in the core. Each ring's gates open only outwards and never for the ring's own colour, so the balls sort themselves. Then they mix again and the loop starts over.
ColourSort.csPresetTip: Ready-made sorts. Each sets the navy page, glowing balls and the loop HUD too.
ColourSort.csRuleTip: Which balls a gate lets through, and which way. A refused ball bounces off the gate as off an arc.
ColourSort.csHintOutwardNotOwn: The reference: a gate opens outwards for every colour but its ring's own, so each colour stops at its own ring.
ColourSort.csHintOutwardOwnOnly: Reversed: a gate opens outwards only for its ring's own colour – the core keeps every other colour.
ColourSort.csHintBothWaysNotOwn: A gate opens both ways for every colour but its ring's own, so sorted balls wander back in: the sort never completes but settles at an equilibrium (roughly half the balls home), and the cycle ends once the count stops rising, on the minor chord. Find Simulation has no sort to search here.
ColourSort.csColoursTip: Colours – and rings: a gated ring for every colour but the last, inside the outer wall. Any number from 2 can be typed (past eight the colours are hues around the wheel).
ColourSort.csPerColourTip: Balls of every colour. Any number from 1 can be typed; a run holds at most 20,000 balls in all.
ColourSort.csBallCeiling: A run holds at most {max} balls: {perColour} of each colour.
ColourSort.csGatesTip: Gates in every gated ring, evenly spaced; every arc between them has a white pin at each end.
ColourSort.csGateWidthTip: A gate's angular width. As wide as the gap between two gates, the ring is all gate.
ColourSort.csSpinTip: How fast the innermost ring turns, in degrees a second; every ring further out turns at the falloff times the ring inside it.
ColourSort.csFalloffTip: Each ring's spin as a share of the ring inside it (0.8: every ring a fifth slower).
ColourSort.csSpeedTip: The balls' constant speed, in px a second of a 720-wide frame (its outer ring is 304 px).
ColourSort.csSizeTip: A ball's radius in px of a 720-wide frame: the solid dot is half of it, the glow the rest.
ColourSort.csContactsTip: On by default: the balls bounce off each other. Off: a ghost gas where every ball meets only the rings, so thousands of balls stay cheap.
ColourSort.csRemixTip: Seconds the remix lasts: the gates stop filtering and a spring pulls every ball back to its place in the first frame, so a recording loops seamlessly.
ColourSort.csLimitTip: The sort ends at this second even with balls still out of their bands (on a minor chord), and the remix starts. With Both ways it usually ends sooner, once the count stops rising.
ColourSort.csFlashTip: A short flash where a gate or an arc turns a ball back.
ColourSort.csLoopNote: Every cycle sorts the balls, holds the bullseye for half a second and mixes them back into the first frame: with Export whole loops on, a recording ends on a seam and loops forever.

BeatMachine.canvasSubtitleStairs: one hop a beat, every landing a note / then the track brings the ball back
BeatMachine.canvasSubtitleMarbles: each marble leaves its tube just in time / to land on its bar on the beat
BeatMachine.desc: Music machines where every note is a ball landing on its target exactly on the beat, with a return path so the machine loops forever. The bars and steps follow the Sound section's scale and root.
BeatMachine.bmPresetTip: Eight steps: the staircase, 8 notes at 80 BPM. Scale staircase: 16 steps playing the scale. Marble xylophone: 10 bars, a seeded original tune at 100 BPM. Load your melody: the marbles play the melody loaded under Sound.
BeatMachine.bmVariantTip: The marble xylophone (tubes, tuned bars, a floor, a lift and a top rail) or the musical staircase (one ball hopping a step a beat, then round the return track).
BeatMachine.bmBpmTip: Beats a minute. Every strike or landing is solved backwards from its beat, so any tempo lands on time: 100 suits the marbles, 80 the staircase.
BeatMachine.loopNoteStairs: {steps} steps and {back} return beats: a loop of {beats} beats, {loop}s.
BeatMachine.bmSourceTip: Where the tune comes from: an original phrase written by the seed, a scale run, the melody loaded under Sound, or a list you type.
BeatMachine.sourceOriginalHint: A new original tune for every seed: Find Simulation can look for one without spare marbles, or the busiest.
BeatMachine.sourceScaleHint: The marbles run up the bars and back down; the staircase plays its ladder, a step a degree.
BeatMachine.sourceMelodyHint: One note a beat from the melody loaded under Sound, each on the bar nearest its pitch. With no melody loaded the original phrase plays.
BeatMachine.sourceCustomHint: One token a beat: a bar or degree number (1 is the lowest), a note name like C4 or F#5, or - for a rest.
BeatMachine.bmNotesTip: One token a beat, separated by spaces or commas: a bar number (1 = the lowest bar), a note name (C4, F#5, Bb3) or - for a rest. The list repeats to fill the loop.
BeatMachine.bmStepsTip: Step bars on the staircase: one note each, so the phrase has as many notes as steps.
BeatMachine.bmStepDxTip: How far each step sits to the right of the last, % of the panel.
BeatMachine.bmStepDyTip: How far each step sits below the last, % of the panel. The hop's arc is solved from it and the beat.
BeatMachine.bmReturnTip: Beats from the hook to the first step again: the ball rolls round the track and is tipped back on just as the phrase starts over. Under 2 it flies straight back.
BeatMachine.bmBarsTip: Tuned bars, low to high from left to right, each with its own tube of marbles in its colour.
BeatMachine.bmDropTip: The fall from a tube to its bar, % of the panel: a marble leaves √(2h/g) before its note.
BeatMachine.bmReboundTip: How high a marble bounces off its bar, as a share of its impact speed, before it falls through the gap to the floor.
BeatMachine.bmPerTubeTip: Marbles each tube holds. Auto: as many as the tune needs. A tube whose marble cannot be back before its next note starts with a spare.
BeatMachine.bmLoopBeatsTip: Beats in the marble machine's loop: 32 at 100 BPM is 19.2 s.
BeatMachine.bmBassTip: A soft bass note every two bars on the lowest note of the phrase there.
BeatMachine.bmCounterTip: Shows the notes of the current loop in the loop HUD ("12 / 32 notes").

WaveTank.canvasSubtitle: every gap sends out its own ripples / crest on crest rises, crest on trough goes still
WaveTank.canvasSubtitlePoints: each source sends out rings of ripples / where a crest meets a trough the water stays still
WaveTank.desc: A ripple tank seen from the front. Straight waves hit a barrier with one, two or seven gaps, then spread, cross into stripes or leave as beams. Each bell rings as loud as the water under it.
WaveTank.wtPresetTip: Double slit: 1, 2, then 7 gaps over a 30 s loop. Single-slit width sweep: one gap growing wider. Grating 15: fifteen gaps. Two sources: no barrier. Talbot carpet: a fine grating seen from higher up.
WaveTank.wtModelTip: Grid: the water moves cell by cell, right up to the gaps. Huygens sum: every gap acts as a row of tiny sources whose ripples add up. It is lighter, and exact far from the gaps.
WaveTank.wtSourceTip: Wave-maker: a bar along the back sends straight crests at the barrier. Point sources: no barrier, just a small source bobbing where each gap would be.
WaveTank.wtGapsTip: The barrier's gap counts in order, one section each, e.g. 1, 2, 7. Give a section its own length with @: 1@11, 2@9, 7@10. The loop is all the sections together.
WaveTank.loopNote: Loop: {loop} s · sections {sections} · the label changes at {changes} s
WaveTank.wtSectionTip: Seconds a section lasts when its entry gives no length of its own.
WaveTank.wtWrapTip: Seconds of the first section moved to the end of the loop. The clip then starts mid-section and ends on the same picture.
WaveTank.wtWidthTip: How wide each gap is, in wavelengths. A narrow gap fans out wide, a wide one lets a straight beam through.
WaveTank.wtWidthEndTip: Grows the gaps from Gap width in the first section to this width in the last. 0 keeps every section the same.
WaveTank.wtSpacingTip: Distance between the centres of neighbouring gaps, in wavelengths. Wider spacing packs the stripes closer together.
WaveTank.wtWavelengthTip: Length of one wave as a share of the tank's width. The source's pitch is rounded so a whole number of waves fits the loop.
WaveTank.wtSpeedTip: How fast the crests travel. 1 is 0.3 tank widths a second.
WaveTank.wtDampingTip: How much the water calms the waves as they travel. 0 is not at all.
WaveTank.wtColsTip: Cells across the tank, with the rows at 4 : 3. More cells look finer and take longer. A grid past about 4 million cells is made smaller.
WaveTank.wtBellsTip: Bells along the front edge, low to high from left to right. Each one rings as loud as the water moves under it.
WaveTank.wtScanRateTip: Strikes a second as the cursor sweeps back and forth along the bells.
WaveTank.wtRidgesTip: How many lines draw the water, from the back to the front.
WaveTank.wtTiltTip: How steeply the camera looks down at the tank. 0° is from the side.
WaveTank.wtBassTip: A quiet bass note under the bells that changes with every section.
WaveTank.wtLabelTip: Shows the gap count of the current section under the tank. Turns the loop HUD on.

BrickRebuild.canvasTitle: smash the logo, then fix it
BrickRebuild.canvasSubtitle: {every, plural, =0 {one touch breaks a brick} one {a new ball for every brick broken} other {a new ball for every # bricks broken}}
BrickRebuild.canvasTitleCapsules: catch the gold, multiply the balls
BrickRebuild.canvasSubtitleCapsules: every gold capsule the paddle catches splits every ball into {split}
BrickRebuild.canvasTitleKaleidoscope: {real, plural, one {only # of these balls is real} other {only # of these balls are real}}
BrickRebuild.canvasSubtitleKaleidoscope: {others, plural, one {the other one is a reflection} other {the other # are reflections}}
BrickRebuild.canvasSubtitleRotate: {others, plural, one {the other one is a copy turned round the centre} other {the other # are copies turned round the centre}}
BrickRebuild.desc: A picture of bricks fills the top of the box. Every brick a ball touches breaks, and every few breaks add a ball. At 0 bricks the picture flies back together colour by colour, and it all starts again.
BrickRebuild.brPresetTip: Smash the emblem: 30 × 30 bricks, 3 balls, a new ball every 4 breaks, at the reference clip's pace. Avalanche: a new ball every break. Big picture: 100 × 100 bricks from your upload. Classic breakout: 1 ball and a paddle, no multiplying. Gold capsules: the paddle catches capsules that triple every ball. Kaleidoscope: 2 real balls and their mirror images in a mosaic.
BrickRebuild.brPictureTip: What the bricks show: the built-in emblem (in the kaleidoscope a mandala), your own uploaded picture, or text you type. The picture only colours the bricks; it never changes how they break.
BrickRebuild.brUploadTip: A logo or any picture: it is cover-fitted into the grid and reduced to at most 8 colours. It stays in this browser – it is never uploaded and never part of a link, a preset or a project file.
BrickRebuild.uploadNone: No picture loaded: the emblem plays until you choose one.
BrickRebuild.uploadError: That file is not a picture the browser can open.
BrickRebuild.brTextTip: Up to 40 characters, drawn in pixel letters across the grid (more columns make sharper letters).
BrickRebuild.brColsTip: Bricks across the picture. Any number from 4 up; the grid holds at most 40,000 bricks (past that it keeps its shape at that many).
BrickRebuild.brRowsTip: Bricks down the picture. Any number from 2 up.
BrickRebuild.brWallTip: How much of the box the bricks fill, from the top (%). The balls start in the space under them.
BrickRebuild.brBallsTip: The balls each loop starts with, near the bottom centre, launched upward.
BrickRebuild.brEveryTip: A new ball appears at the broken brick every this many breaks (0: never). The board holds at most 2,000 balls; past that the breaks still count.
BrickRebuild.brSpeedTip: px a second at a 720-wide clip. The balls keep this speed through the whole smash.
BrickRebuild.brSizeTip: Radius in px at a 720-wide clip. Collisions are swept, so no ball slips through a brick at any speed or size.
BrickRebuild.brHpTip: Touches a brick takes before it breaks; a damaged brick shows lighter.
BrickRebuild.brDurationTip: If bricks are still standing after this many seconds, the rebuild starts anyway.
BrickRebuild.brSettleTip: Seconds the balls fall to the floor under gravity once the last brick breaks.
BrickRebuild.brRebuildTip: Seconds the bricks take to fly back in; the counter climbs back to the total, the balls fade and the start balls reappear.
BrickRebuild.brOrderTip: Colour layers: the biggest colour first (the field, then the ring, then the accent), each from the middle out. Random: a seeded order. Rows: from the bottom row up.
BrickRebuild.brDropTip: The kick and pad groove starts on the first bar line after this many seconds (the Sound section's tempo) and stops at 0 bricks.
BrickRebuild.brBedTip: A soft pad, a sub and a kick on every beat under the brick plucks. Off: only the plucks, the whoosh and the bell.
BrickRebuild.brCapsulesTip: Broken bricks may drop gold capsules; a paddle above the floor runs to catch them, and every catch splits every ball in play.
BrickRebuild.brCapsuleChanceTip: The chance that a broken brick drops a capsule.
BrickRebuild.brSplitTip: How many balls each ball becomes when the paddle catches a capsule (3: from 3 balls to 9, 27, 81…).
BrickRebuild.brSymmetryTip: Off at 1. Above it the bricks form a round mosaic with a hole, the real balls move in one wedge and are drawn with all their images, and every brick hit is copied to its images – the picture breaks symmetrically.
BrickRebuild.brSymmetryModeTip: Mirror: the wedge has mirror walls and the images are reflections (an odd number doubles). Rotate: the images are copies turned round the centre.
BrickRebuild.brHoleTip: The empty middle of the kaleidoscope's mosaic, % of its radius.
BrickRebuild.kaleidoscopeNote: {real, plural, one {# real ball} other {# real balls}}, {shown} drawn.
BrickRebuild.brOutlineTip: White balls with a thin dark rim, as in the reference clip. Off: the balls use your ball look (colour, picture, faces).

DrawingMachine.canvasSubtitleHarmonograph: friction shrinks it toward the middle / a 2% detune keeps it twisting
DrawingMachine.canvasSubtitleOrbits: a line between them every few days / a mark each time they line up
DrawingMachine.desc: Two machines that draw one figure and then start over, so every clip loops. Three pendulums swing one pen across paper, or two planets draw a flower with a line every few days.
DrawingMachine.dmPresetTip: Three pendulums, one pen: the reference harmonograph (1.5 Hz, 2% apart, a rotary swing at twice the rate). Lissajous 3:2: two swings at 2:3, no rotary one. Decay rose: a strong rotary swing and quick friction. Earth and Venus: 13 : 8, eight years, the pentagram. Earth and Mars: their real periods, so the pattern creeps round. Jupiter and Saturn: 5 : 2, a triangle.
DrawingMachine.dmMachineTip: The harmonograph (three damped pendulums drive one pen over a sheet of paper) or the orbits (two planets round the Sun, a straight line joining them every few days).
DrawingMachine.loopNoteHarmonograph: {draw}s of drawing and a {scroll}s paper scroll: a loop of {loop}s.
DrawingMachine.loopNoteOrbits: {draw}s of drawing, a {hold}s hold and a {rewind}s rewind: a loop of {loop}s.
DrawingMachine.dmFreqTip: How many times a second the left-right pendulum swings. The up-down one swings a little faster (the detune) and the rotary one at a multiple of it.
DrawingMachine.dmDetuneTip: How much faster the up-down pendulum swings than the left-right one, in %. At 0 the figure closes on itself. At 2% they drift in and out of step, so the shape keeps twisting.
DrawingMachine.dmRotaryTip: The rotary pendulum's rate as a multiple of the left-right one's: it moves the pen round in a circle. 0 stops it.
DrawingMachine.dmDampingTip: Seconds for the swings to fall to about a third (e^−1): friction shrinks the drawing toward the middle. 18 s leaves it at about 30% after 22 s.
DrawingMachine.dmAmpXTip: How far the left-right pendulum moves the pen, % of the figure's radius (100 reaches the paper's edge).
DrawingMachine.dmAmpYTip: How far the up-down pendulum moves the pen, % of the figure's radius.
DrawingMachine.dmAmpRTip: The radius of the rotary pendulum's circle, % of the figure's radius.
DrawingMachine.dmPhaseTip: Where in its swing the pendulum starts, in degrees: two equal swings 90° apart draw a circle, in step a line.
DrawingMachine.dmDrawTip: Seconds the pen draws before the paper scrolls.
DrawingMachine.dmScrollTip: Seconds the paper takes to scroll a fresh sheet in: the loop's reset. The pendulums start again from the beginning.
DrawingMachine.dmInnerTip: The planet on the inner orbit (its colour, its name in the title and its real period when Exact ratio is off).
DrawingMachine.dmOuterTip: The planet on the outer orbit. The conjunction marks sit on its orbit.
DrawingMachine.dmExactTip: On: the inner planet goes round p times while the outer one goes round q, so the flower closes exactly and the loop is seamless. Off: the planets keep their real periods and the pattern creeps round a little every cycle.
DrawingMachine.dmRatioPTip: Orbits of the inner planet in one cycle (Venus: 13).
DrawingMachine.dmRatioQTip: Orbits of the outer planet in one cycle (Earth: 8). The planets line up p − q times a cycle.
DrawingMachine.dmRadiusTip: The inner orbit's radius as a share of the outer one's (Venus : Earth = 0.723).
DrawingMachine.dmLineDaysTip: Days between two lines joining the planets. Fewer days, a denser flower.
DrawingMachine.dmYearsTip: Years drawn before the hold and the rewind. 8 closes the 13 : 8 flower.
DrawingMachine.dmSecPerYearTip: How long one year takes on screen: at 1.8 s eight years draw in 14.4 s.
DrawingMachine.dmHoldTip: Seconds the finished flower holds before the rewind.
DrawingMachine.dmRewindTip: Seconds the rewind takes: the year counts back to 0.0 and the lines un-draw, newest first, so the clip loops.
DrawingMachine.dmPentagramTip: Joins the conjunction marks in order: five marks 144° apart make a pentagram.
DrawingMachine.dmInkTip: The colour ramp the drawing drifts through over a cycle: Auto is the machine's own (violet to crimson ink on paper, blue to magenta light in space).
DrawingMachine.dmSoundTip: Harmonograph: a drone that breathes with the pendulums' energy, the pen's scratch and the paper's ratchet. Orbits: a soft groove, a pluck at every conjunction and a wash on the rewind.

PerfectFit.desc: Pieces drop straight down into a box until it is exactly full. Every piece placed plays the next note up. Pick the 12 pentominoes or Tetris perfect clears.
PerfectFit.pfPresetTip: Three rectangles: the 12 pentominoes into 10 × 6, 12 × 5 and 15 × 4. Every piece fits: Tetris, four four-line clears and a twelve-line finale (70 pieces). Speed run: the rectangles at 0.15 s a piece. Big well: Tetris in a 20 × 40 well.
PerfectFit.pfVariantTip: Pentominoes: the 12 shapes of five squares, each used once, fill three rectangles. Tetris: tetrominoes fill whole lines of a well and clear them.
PerfectFit.pfPieceSecTip: How long each piece takes from the tray to its landing. In Tetris it is the first section's: every later section is a little faster.
PerfectFit.pfFallTip: How a piece covers the last stretch: 0 is a constant speed, 1 a fall under gravity from rest, higher values a later, harder landing.
PerfectFit.pfBeatTip: Every landing on the beat of the Sound section's tempo: a piece takes the power of two of beats nearest Seconds per piece, each completion whole beats, the loop whole bars.
PerfectFit.beatNote: Landings on the beat of {bpm} BPM (the Sound section's tempo).
PerfectFit.pfSeedTip: Which way of filling the boxes you see. Auto picks a new one every run. A number keeps that solution, and Find Simulation can set it.
PerfectFit.pfBoxesTip: The rectangles in order, width × height in cells, such as 10×6, 12×5, 15×4. The 12 pentominoes cover exactly 60 squares, so a box of another size stays empty.
PerfectFit.boxNoteWays: {w} × {h}: one of {ways, number} ways to fill it.
PerfectFit.boxNoteNoDrop: {w} × {h}: it has tilings, but none can be built by dropping pieces straight down.
PerfectFit.boxNoteNone: {w} × {h}: too thin, the 12 pieces cannot fill it.
PerfectFit.boxNoteSize: {w} × {h} is {area} cells: the 12 pieces need exactly 60.
PerfectFit.boxNoteOther: {w} × {h}: the solver looks for a tiling it can drop.
PerfectFit.pfSectionsTip: Each number is a section of the well that ends in a perfect clear, such as 4,4,4,4,12. A four-line section ends with a vertical I dropping into the last gap.
PerfectFit.pfWellWTip: Columns of the well. Width × lines must be a multiple of 4, or that section is left out.
PerfectFit.pfWellHTip: Rows of the well; it grows to hold its tallest section.
PerfectFit.pfHoldTip: The last section keeps its full rows until its last piece lands, then clears them all at once. Off: it clears four lines at a time.

PerfectFit.canvasLines: {count, plural, one {# line cleared} other {# lines cleared}}

about.long: {siteName} is a free ball physics studio that runs in the browser, with no account and nothing to install. It began with a simple problem. Bouncing-ball videos were everywhere, and every way to make one was slow. Now a creator can open a tab, pick one of {count} modes, tune the physics and export a vertical video for TikTok, Reels or Shorts. Every mode, setting and export is free. Free clips carry a small watermark, and Pro removes it for {monthly} a month or {yearly} a year. A Windows app adds GPU video encoding, a render queue and an AI studio that plans clips and writes captions. {siteName} is a small independent project, available in English, Polish and Spanish.
